Honest opinion, no sugar-coating: **the dashboard half of your idea is genuinely good and builds directly on what we just made. The IDE and voice-bot halves would quietly kill your class.** Let me take it apart piece by piece.

## What's strong

**The observability dashboard is the natural next consumer of the data lake.** We just built a system that emits sessions, spec states, gate decisions, assurance verdicts, counterexamples, and deploy metrics as structured events — a dashboard is exactly what that exhaust is *for*. Seeing the pipeline state ("002 requirements: awaiting-review, verdict 85%"), session history, and event streams in one place would genuinely improve the workflow. No reservations about this part.

**The memory-allocation visualization is the best idea in the whole message** — and I don't think you realize why. Rust has no GC, so there's no runtime that hands you allocation stats; to visualize allocations, *we'd have to instrument the allocator ourselves*. That means writing a wrapping `GlobalAlloc` — a tracking allocator crate that logs every alloc/dealloc as envelope events into the same data lake. Writing that is maybe the single best hands-on lesson in Rust memory management that exists: you'd literally *watch* a `String` allocate on the heap, watch ownership move without copying, and watch `Drop` free it at scope end. The visualization becomes a teaching instrument, not just a pretty chart. I'd promote this to a first-class curriculum item.

## Where I'd push back

**The "small IDE": don't build it.** A real editing experience means Monaco + rust-analyzer + a compile backend — weeks of TypeScript and infrastructure work that teaches you zero Rust, to produce a worse VS Code. The 90% substitute at 2% of the cost: read-only code panes with syntax highlighting in the dashboard, linking out to GitHub. You already have editors; the dashboard's job is *seeing*, not editing.

**Voice chat: don't build it either, at least not now.** Real-time voice is a serious engineering project (streaming STT/TTS, latency management, audio infra) — again, none of it Rust. And you already talk to me by voice through the Claude apps; your voice-to-text prompts are how this whole project started. Building a second, worse voice channel to the same brain has near-zero return. If you ever want it, it's a fine *late-stage* Unit of Work — after the four compute targets are mastered.

**The honest meta-risk:** this is the second consecutive idea that grows the *tooling around* the class rather than the class. Pipeline v2 + data lake were worth it — they're leverage. But you haven't written a line of Rust yet, and the full version of this idea (product-grade UI/UX + IDE + voice) is months of mostly-TypeScript work. The failure mode of ambitious learning projects is always the same: the scaffolding becomes the project. I'd hate to watch goldeneye become a dashboard company.

## The version I'd actually build

Scoped so every layer either teaches Rust or ships in hours, not weeks:

1. **v0 — today, zero infrastructure:** I generate the dashboard as a Claude **Artifact** — a self-contained page rendering the current lake (pipeline states, sessions, event timeline). Regenerated on demand. Free, instant, disposable.
2. **v1 — static dashboard, serverless (Wave 2 extension):** a static site on S3 + CloudFront using **DuckDB-WASM in the browser** to query `goldeneye-lake` Parquet directly — no backend at all. Modern, genuinely elegant, and it teaches the S3/columnar material already in SKILLS 2e.
3. **v2 — the tracking allocator** (`goldeneye-alloc` crate) feeding allocation timelines into the lake; the dashboard grows a memory panel. This is the crown jewel, and it's ~pure Rust.
4. **v3 (optional, later):** a small `axum` backend for live tailing — which conveniently is your Fargate curriculum item wearing a useful costume.

Each of these goes through the pipeline as its own spec, so you'd gate each layer before I build it.

That's my honest read: keep the dashboard and the allocator viz, cut the IDE, defer the voice bot, and sequence it so the Rust always outweighs the TypeScript. If that reshaping works for you, the cheapest way to make it concrete is the v0 artifact — say the word and I'll render one from the lake as it stands (it only has a handful of events yet, but you'll see the bones). Or if you disagree — especially about the IDE or voice — tell me what job you need them to do that existing tools don't, and I'll re-plan around that.
